The ring itself and the C-N, C-C, C-O bond lengths are broadly similar in every conformer, so ring strain and local bond-length strain are not the main differentiators. The dominant geometric feature is the orientation of the CH2OH group and especially the O-H bond relative to the tertiary ring nitrogen. Several conformers place the O-H hydrogen between O and N with O-N about 2.7-2.9 Å, H-N about 2.1-2.4 Å, and a reasonably linear O-H...N arrangement; these are assigned a meaningful intramolecular hydrogen-bond stabilization. Conformers with H-N longer than about 2.5 Å and smaller O-H...N linearity have only a weak or uncertain hydrogen bond. Conformers with the OH pointing away from N and O-N >3.5 Å lack this interaction but are usually more open and have fewer close nonbonded contacts. Within the hydrogen-bonded group, I prioritized shorter H-N, better O-H...N linearity, and fewer tight C-O or C...O contacts (for example C3-O or C2-O contacts approaching 2.9 Å). Conformers 28, 6, 11, 25, 26, 19, 20, 3, 24, 17, 2, 21, 14 and 27 form the top block because all have a usable O-H...N hydrogen bond and no obvious severe clash. Near the bottom of that block, 27 is a borderline hydrogen-bonded form because its H-N is somewhat longer, and 14/21 are slightly more compact in the propyl/OH region. The next conformers, 9, 8, 5 and 10, put the oxygen near nitrogen and the hydrogen somewhat toward it, but the H bond is weaker or less linear than the top group; they likely beat very open non-hydrogen-bonded forms, but the differences are small. The remaining no-hydrogen-bond conformers, 18, 13, 12, 23, 29, 15, 22 and 4, are mostly open and lack close O...N or C...O clashes; they are ordered by subtle C3-O and overall rotamer compactness. Finally, 16, 30, 7 and 1 have the oxygen near nitrogen but a poorly aligned or very long O-H...N interaction, so they are treated as having the least clear favorable interaction and are placed near the bottom. The ordering inside the last several entries is genuinely uncertain because the penalties and stabilizers are all small compared with the clearly hydrogen-bonded conformers.

These are therefore clearly the most stable. For the remaining structures, the closest OH...O contacts are generally >3.3 A and usually >4.5 A, so no comparable strong hydrogen bond is present; their relative order is much more subtle. I then used the side-chain C(ring)-CH2-CH2-O torsion as a proxy for whether the tether is anti/extended or gauche/folded, and combined that with O...O distance and short H...O approach. Conformers 14, 21, 9, 18, 22, 10, and 20 have nearly anti extended side-chain/tether geometries and no bad close OH contacts, so they rank next. Conformer 17 is intermediate anti/gauche and is placed just below them. The next tier consists of reasonably staggered, less compact gauche rotamers: 16, 1, 4, 28, 8, 24, 12, and 2. They are less stable than the anti-extended set but more stable than the more crowded, less ideal torsion states. The middle-to-low group includes 26, 7, 27, 6, 3, and 29, where the side-chain torsion is less ideal and/or the oxygens are folded closer without forming a strong hydrogen bond. The lowest group is 13, 15, 23, and 5: these are compact but not strongly hydrogen bonded or have the least favorable side-chain torsional alignment, with 5 placed last because it has no hydrogen bond and a poorer O-C-C-C alignment. The order outside the top four is uncertain and should be regarded as a geometry-based approximation rather than a quantitative energy ranking.

Because the aziridine strain, alkyne unsaturation, and basic bond framework are common to all 30 structures, the ranking is dominated by torsional and nonbonded differences: carbonyl O orientation relative to the CH2 groups and alkyne, N-H orientation, and close contacts involving the aziridine CH2/ring substituents. I used approximate geometric penalties: (1) compact O...C3 contacts, which can create carbonyl/CH2 crowding, seen most clearly in 7, 23, 6, and 13; (2) compact O...C4/O...C5 contacts, which can create carbonyl/alkyne crowding, especially in 1, 6, 20, and 28; (3) N...O compactness without a short N-H...O geometry, suggesting nonproductive folding rather than a strong intramolecular H bond, most relevant to 1, 6, and 28; (4) close alkyne/ring contacts, especially C5...C7 being unusually short in 14, and somewhat shorter in 9 and 20; and (5) mildly close N-H...alkyne contacts in 19, 8, 5, and 18, which I treated as slightly stabilizing or at least not destabilizing.
